Not with this codebase: bsky.app/the reference PDS can't store custom reaction records. You would need to run your own PDS and AppView and add your own lexicon. A fallback for other clients only works if you build it yourself.

- **The PDS rejects unvalidated writes.** `com.atproto.repo.createRecord` throws "Unvalidated writes are not yet supported." when `validate === false` (`createRecord.ts:31`). So you can't write a record with an unknown collection by skipping validation.
- **Unknown lexicons fail validation.** With validation on, `prepareCreate` calls `assertValidRecord` (`pds/src/repo/prepare.ts:109-125`). That calls `lex.lexicons.assertValidRecord`, and a `LexiconDefNotFoundError` for an unregistered `$type` is turned into an `InvalidRecordError`. The PDS only accepts collections whose lexicons are compiled in (`app.bsky.feed.like`, `repost`, `post` and so on).
- **The AppView only indexes the lexicons it knows.** The indexing processor validates each record against its own lexicon (`bsky/src/services/indexing/processor.ts:60-61`) and skips records that fail. The `getPostThread`, `getTimeline` and `PostView` output schemas have no field for custom reactions. Custom records wouldn't be indexed, and they wouldn't appear in any bsky.app view.

**What to build:**
1. Define a lexicon for your reaction record, for example `com.yourapp.feed.reaction` with a `subject` strongRef and a `reaction` string.
2. Run a PDS fork or config that registers that lexicon, so users' repos can hold the records. Or accept the records on a PDS you control.
3. Run an AppView or indexer that consumes `subscribeRepos` and indexes your collection. Expose it through your own XRPC endpoints, for example `com.yourapp.feed.getReactions`, and optionally use it to hydrate posts.
4. For other clients, treat the reactions as an enhancement. Stock clients will ignore them, so the fallback is the existing `app.bsky.feed.like` records.

The like lexicon is the closest existing model for the record shape.

You can't derive the URL client-side: the first path segment is an HMAC signature (base64url of HMAC(key, salt + path)) made with the server's secret key and salt. The rest is `/rs:fit:2000:2000:1:0/plain/<did>/<cid>@jpeg`. ImageUriBuilder.getSignedPath builds it, and the 'feed_fullsize' and 'feed_thumbnail' presets of getCommonSignedUri set the sizes. Instead of building it, fetch the post through the AppView (for example getPostThread or getTimeline). The hydrated embed view (app.bsky.embed.images#view) returns signed `thumb` and `fullsize` URLs. For the raw blob, use com.atproto.sync.getBlob with the did and cid.

The original isn't lost. The upload keeps the original blob unmodified. The 1000px and 2000px sizes are not stored. They are generated on request by the image CDN/resizer, using the presets in `ImageUriBuilder.getCommonSignedUri`. `feed_thumbnail` is `fit: 'inside'` at 1000x1000, and `feed_fullsize` is `fit: 'inside'` at 2000x2000. Both set `min: true`, and in `image/sharp.ts` that sets `withoutEnlargement: min !== true`, which is `false`. That setting lets small images be upscaled, which is the blurry result you're seeing.

To get the original, read the blob CID from the post record, at `embed.images[].image.ref`. Then fetch it with `com.atproto.sync.getBlob` (`?did=<repo did>&cid=<cid>`). That returns the raw uploaded bytes, so you can read the real width and height from the image itself.

The `app.bsky.embed.images` view only returns the `thumb` and `fullsize` URLs. It has no width or height fields, so a client can't get the dimensions from the API. A client has to either download the original blob or load the image and use its natural size. To avoid upscaling, a client can cap the displayed size at the image's natural dimensions. A lexicon change that stores the dimensions would also fix it, but nothing like that exists in this code.

You don't need to convert the BlobRef yourself. The server builds the thumb and fullsize URLs from the author DID plus the image CID with `imgUriBuilder.getCommonSignedUri('feed_thumbnail' | 'feed_fullsize', did, cid)`. If you only have the raw BlobRef, you can fetch the bytes with `com.atproto.sync.getBlob`, using the author DID and the blob CID.

The code doesn't special-case `*.bsky.social` inside the handle resolver itself. `HandleResolver` in `packages/identity/src/handle/index.ts` only tries DNS TXT (`_atproto.<handle>`) and HTTPS (`/.well-known/atproto-did`). A hosted-domain handle has to be resolved by asking a PDS or appview that serves `com.atproto.identity.resolveHandle`.

That endpoint is implemented in the PDS handler at `packages/pds/src/api/com/atproto/identity/resolveHandle.ts`. It works like this:
- It first looks the handle up in the PDS's own account database (`getAccount`). A hit returns that account's DID.
- If there is no hit and the handle ends with one of the PDS's `availableUserDomains`, it fails with "Unable to resolve handle". A handle on a hosted domain is expected to be in that PDS's database.
- For any other handle, it asks the appview's `resolveHandle`, if one is configured. If that fails, it falls back to DNS/HTTPS resolution through `idResolver.handle.resolve`.

So the answer to your question is the second option: use a service's `com.atproto.identity.resolveHandle` for these handles. Don't expect DNS or HTTPS to work for them. I didn't find code that checks `describeServer` and `availableUserDomains` on a parent domain, so that approach isn't implemented here. It is only an idea in your question.

The repo's README says AT Protocol means "Authenticated Transfer Protocol". The repo is the working implementation of it, and Bluesky is an app built on top of it. For a beginner, the README recommends starting with the Overview Guide at https://atproto.com/guides/overview. The code shows how the layers fit together:

- Lexicons, which are schemas, define the methods and record types. They use reverse-DNS names, with `com.atproto.*` for the core protocol and `app.bsky.*` for the Bluesky social app (posts, likes and follows).
- Clients talk to servers through XRPC routes under `/xrpc/`.

The blob is broken because `curl -F` uploads it as multipart/form-data, and uploadBlob stores the raw request body as the blob. The lexicon (`lexicons/com/atproto/repo/uploadBlob.json`) declares the input as `*/*`, so there is no multipart parsing. The handler passes `input.encoding` and `input.body` straight to `addUntetheredBlob` (`pds/src/api/com/atproto/repo/uploadBlob.ts`, line 11). The multipart boundary and headers therefore end up saved inside the blob, and getBlob serves those bytes back, which is not a valid JPEG.

Send the file bytes as the request body with the correct image content type. With curl that is `--data-binary @test.jpg -H "Content-Type: image/jpeg"`. Also use `image/jpeg` rather than `image/jpg`. In CFML/Java, post the raw bytes as the body instead of a form-file part.

I didn't run this against the PDS, and I didn't open `addUntetheredBlob` to check how it stores the stream.

My take is that Lexicon is its own thing that happens to look like JSON Schema. I'd implement it from scratch and only borrow small pieces.

This repo has no JSON Schema machinery at all. A search for "json schema", "ajv" and "jsonschema" finds nothing. The `@atproto/lexicon` package validates with its own hand-written code. `validators/complex.ts` dispatches on the Lexicon `type` field (boolean, integer, string, bytes, cid-link, unknown, object, array, blob). `primitives.ts`, `blob.ts`, `formats.ts` and `xrpc.ts` carry the rest.

`zod` is only used to validate the shape of the Lexicon documents themselves, in `types.ts`. It isn't used to validate data against them.

The surface still resembles JSON Schema. Both use `type`, `properties`, `required`, `enum`, `const`, `default`, `minimum`/`maximum`, `minLength`/`maxLength`, and `items` for arrays. The resemblance stops there, for these reasons:

- **Different type vocabulary.**
  - `token`, `blob`, `bytes`, `cid-link` and `unknown` have no JSON Schema equivalent.
  - `integer` is the only numeric type.
  - `record`, `query`, `procedure` and `subscription` describe repo records and XRPC endpoints, not just data.
- **Refs are not `$ref`.** A `ref` is an NSID-style reference (`lexicon.id#def`) resolved through a `Lexicons` registry. `union` is a list of refs with a `closed` flag, where open unions allow unknown types. It is not `oneOf`.
- **Strict, closed grammar.** Every definition is `.strict()` and only a small keyword set is allowed. There are no `allOf`, `anyOf`, `if/then`, `patternProperties`, `additionalProperties` or `pattern` keywords.
- **Different semantics for some keywords.**
  - `nullable` is a list of property names on the object. In JSON Schema it is part of the type.
  - `knownValues` is an open enum.
  - String lengths come in two forms, bytes (`minLength`/`maxLength`) and graphemes (`minGraphemes`/`maxGraphemes`).
  - String `format` values are atproto-specific: `did`, `handle`, `at-uri`, `nsid`, `cid`, `language`, `at-identifier`.
- **Data model.** Values can be IPLD types such as bytes, CID links and blob refs. Plain JSON has no such types.

If I were in a language with mature JSON Schema libraries, I wouldn't customize one. You'd be fighting its keyword set and `$ref` resolution, and it would accept constructs Lexicon forbids. Lexicon's validator is small, roughly a switch over about ten types plus a ref resolver, so writing it directly is easier. I'd only borrow the pieces that don't depend on Lexicon's structure, such as RFC 3339 datetime and URI parsing and Unicode grapheme counting.

Compared with a JSON Schema library, schema-to-code generation is a bigger job. The `lex-cli` package does it, and it matters more than the validator.

Sessions are per-client, not per-browser. An app logs in itself with com.atproto.server.createSession (handle or email plus password or app password) and gets back access and refresh JWTs. It can then call com.atproto.server.getSession ("Get information about the current session"), which needs that access token and returns { handle, did, email }. The @atproto/api AtpAgent wraps both calls and keeps the session in `agent.session`, which includes the DID. There is no cross-site session to read. This snapshot of the code has no Ozone, no external-labeler ingestion and no per-request labeler selection (no `atproto-accept-labelers`). The appview only reads labels from its own local `label` table. `getLabelsForUris` runs `selectFrom('label').where('uri','in',subjects)`, and `getPostThread`, `getPosts` and the feed and actor views build `labels` from it.

Rows in that table are written by the appview's own labeler (`cfg.labelerDid`, from `LABELER_DID`). That happens through its own moderation actions or its automatic labeler. Labels your separate Ozone instance creates, such as `!hide`, never reach bsky.app's appview. That is why `labels` comes back as `[]` and the post looks unchanged.

To debug:
1. Check that your labels exist: query your Ozone's `com.atproto.label.queryLabels`, or look at its label table.
2. Check that the appview actually reads them. Look at the `labels` array in the `getPostThread` response, as you did, and at the `label` table the appview reads.

To get the result you want, use one of these:
- Run your own appview (bsky) and PDS, and point `LABELER_DID` at your labeler, so its label table receives your labels.
- Use a client or appview that supports third-party labelers. It has to subscribe to or accept your labeler's DID.

Reporting the same post twice and adding more labels won't help. The labels are created, but nothing reads them.

Not by passing a foreign handle to createAccount alone. createAccount (ensureValidHandle) calls ensureHandleServiceConstraints against the PDS's availableUserDomains and rejects other domains with UnsupportedDomain unless you also supply your own `did` whose handle already resolves (DNS TXT _atproto.<handle> "did=<did>" or /.well-known/atproto-did) to that DID. Without a did, createAccount builds a did:plc genesis op via plc.createOp (signing key, rotation keys, handle, pds: publicUrl), signed by the PDS's PLC rotation key, and sends it with plcClient.sendOperation. The PDS creates no DNS record itself; it just answers handle resolution for its own domains. Practical route: create the account with a PDS handle, publish the DNS/well-known record for your domain, then call com.atproto.identity.updateHandle, which resolves the external handle, checks it matches the requester's DID, and updates the PLC doc.

The PDS isn't failing by itself. It proxies getProfile to the appview (bsky), because ctx.canProxy(req) is true. The appview returns "Profile not found" when `actorService.getActor` finds no row for that DID or handle in its `actor` table (bsky getProfile.ts:15-18). That `actor` row is only created by the appview's indexing, in `indexHandle` (insertInto('actor')). `indexHandle` runs when the appview's repo subscription (subscription/repo.ts) receives events from the PDS firehose (`com.atproto.sync.subscribeRepos`). To fix it, point the appview's repo subscription (`REPO_PROVIDER`) at your PDS. Make sure the PDS notifies or crawls the appview, then let it index or backfill the account, for example by creating a new post or profile record to trigger an event.

What follows is from my knowledge of the atproto OAuth spec, not from this code.

1. **The PDS URL is not compared to `iss`.** The DID document gives you the PDS URL. You then fetch `<PDS>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`, which lists `authorization_servers`. For an entryway setup, that list contains `https://bsky.social`. You fetch that server's `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` metadata and check that its `issuer` equals the token's `iss` and the server URL you used. So the chain is DID → PDS → resource metadata → auth server → issuer. That is why a PDS host like `gomphus.us-west.host.bsky.network` can sit behind `https://bsky.social`.

2. **Start from an identity, not from the email.** If the user typed a handle or DID, resolve it to a DID first (check the handle ↔ DID link in both directions). Then discover the PDS and auth server from that DID. After the flow, check that the token response's `sub` equals that DID.

3. **Email login happens on the auth server.** If the user logs in with an email there, that has no effect on the check, because `sub` is compared against the DID you resolved at the start. If you started from only a PDS or entryway URL, you have no expected DID. In that case, treat `sub` as untrusted until you have resolved its DID document and confirmed that its PDS's authorization server is the issuer you used.

There is no DPoP form of `refreshSession`. It is a legacy session endpoint and only accepts a plain `Authorization: Bearer <refreshJwt>` header. The PDS `refreshVerifier` (auth.ts:263-271) reads the token with `getToken`, which returns null unless the header starts with `Bearer ` (auth.ts:127-130). A `DPoP <token>` header is therefore treated as missing auth, which gives the `AuthMissing` 401. The `InvalidToken` 400 fits the other case: an OAuth access or refresh token is not a legacy refresh JWT with the refresh scope, so it fails verification. The reference client (agent.ts:260) sends the legacy `refreshJwt` from `createSession` as `Bearer ${refreshJwt}`, with an empty body and no DPoP proof.

OAuth sessions are refreshed differently, at the authorization server's token endpoint. There you send a `grant_type=refresh_token` request with a DPoP proof, using the OAuth refresh token. You don't call `com.atproto.server.refreshSession`.

This codebase has no `invalid_grant` / "Session expired" response. It has no OAuth code at all, so that exact error probably comes from a different or newer server. The nearest equivalent is the PDS `com.atproto.server.refreshSession` endpoint, which returns a 400 `ExpiredToken` with the message "Token has been revoked". It does this when `rotateRefreshToken` returns null (`services/auth.ts`, lines 30-73). That happens in two cases:
1. The refresh token's id isn't in the `refresh_token` table. The token was already deleted: revoked by logout, an app-password revocation, or a revoke-all-by-DID, or cleaned up after it expired.
2. The token's effective expiry has passed. Every time a token is used for refresh, its lifetime is cut down to a 2-hour grace window (`REFRESH_GRACE_MS`) or its original expiry, whichever is sooner. Reusing the same old refresh token after more than 2 hours therefore fails.

So this is an expected, deterministic failure and not a random error. It means the refresh token is no longer valid. Don't retry with the same token. Treat the session as dead and have the user re-authenticate.

A retry is safe only within the 2-hour grace window. In that window the same old token returns the same `nextId`, so a lost response can be recovered. A likely cause of intermittent failures is concurrent or repeated refreshes with a stale token: the client doesn't persist the newly rotated `refreshJwt`, or two workers refresh at once. Always store the new refresh token returned by each refresh.

The code doesn't define a recovery protocol for out-of-order seqs, and it doesn't implement the "keep commit 1 until commit 2 arrives" behaviour you describe. Your reading of "monotonic" matches what the reference PDS does. Its outbox only emits an event if `evt.seq > this.lastSeen`, so it never sends 1, 3, 2 on one connection.

The reference consumer, the bsky appview in `packages/bsky/src/subscription/repo.ts`, has no reordering or gap detection:
- It processes messages per repo and logs any message it can't process, then moves on (lines 60-62). It does this so the cursor doesn't get stuck on a bad message.
- The cursor only advances over the consecutive run of completed messages (`ConsecutiveList` in `util.ts`). This handles messages that finish out of order within the consumer. It doesn't handle out-of-order seqs sent by the server.
- Handling a commit means indexing its ops, so a missing earlier commit isn't repaired by waiting for it.
- Commits flagged `tooBig` or `rebase` trigger a full `indexRepo` of the repo. That is the consumer's only repair path, and it's the same full re-sync a consumer would use if it found itself stuck.

So a consumer that breaks or gets stuck on a bad repo isn't something the code rules out. If a gap is seen, the safe approach is to fetch the repo again, for example with `sync.getRepo` or `getCheckout`. That is my inference. The code doesn't state it.

The code has no locale because it doesn't need one. Grapheme counting here uses the default Unicode extended grapheme cluster rules (UAX #29) through the `Graphemer` library. Those rules are locale-independent, so "e + U+0301" counts as 1 grapheme everywhere. `graphemeLen` creates a plain `new Graphemer()` and calls `countGraphemes(str)`, with no locale parameter. The lexicon validator calls it for `maxGraphemes` and `minGraphemes` (primitives.ts:226 and 238).

The reference validator does not count UTF-16 code units, as the question assumes. The code units appear only in the byte-based `maxLength` and `minLength` checks, which use `utf8Len` on UTF-8 bytes. Those checks sit alongside the grapheme checks in the same validator. Lexicons such as `app.bsky.feed.post` pair `maxGraphemes: 300` with `maxLength: 3000`. The byte limit is a hard bound. The grapheme limit is the user-facing one.

The remaining inconsistency is the Unicode version. Different implementations can still disagree on newer emoji sequences if their segmentation libraries follow different Unicode versions. That is a version difference and has nothing to do with locale.

This is expected. Each event-stream frame is two concatenated CBOR objects: a header followed by a body. The `t` field is in the header, not in the body. An ATProto repo is a signed, content-addressed (CID-linked) Merkle Search Tree (MST) of one account's records, with a chain of signed commits on top of it. The reference implementation is `packages/repo`. Its `Repo` class (`repo.ts`) shows what a PDS has to build:

1. **Records.** Each record is a DAG-CBOR block. Its CID is the hash of its bytes. Records are keyed in the tree as `collection/rkey`, for example `app.bsky.feed.post/<tid>`.

2. **MST (`mst/mst.ts`).**
   - This is the data structure that maps `collection/rkey` to a record CID. It is ordered, deterministic and independent of insert order.
   - Each key is hashed with SHA-256, and the leading zero bits decide which layer the key sits on (2 bits per layer, about 4-way fanout).
   - Each node is a CBOR block of the form `{l: leftmost subtree CID|null, e: [{p: prefix length shared with the previous key, k: key suffix, v: record CID, t: right subtree CID|null}]}`.
   - A node's CID is the hash of its bytes. Changing a leaf therefore changes every node on the path to it and gives a new root CID.

3. **Commit.** This is a signed block `{did, version: 2, prev: CID|null, data: MST root CID, sig}`.
   - `util.signCommit` signs it with the account's repo signing key.
   - `prev` links to the previous commit.
   - The repo's head is the latest commit CID.
   - The first commit has `prev: null`.

4. **Block storage (`storage/`).**
   - `RepoStorage` is a CID-to-bytes store.
   - It keeps the current head and has `applyCommit`, `getBlocks` and `getHead`.
   - It holds the commit, MST node and record blocks.
   - Blobs are stored separately through the `BlobStore` interface.

5. **Writing.**
   - `Repo.formatCommit` applies create, update and delete ops to the MST (`data.add`, `data.update`, `data.delete`).
   - It collects the new record and MST blocks with `getUnstoredBlocks`, and re-adds any blocks that were removed and then re-added in the same commit.
   - It signs a new commit that points to the previous one, and returns `{commit, prev, blocks}`.
   - `applyCommit` persists that data and moves the head. `applyWrites` does both steps.

6. **Creating a repo.** `Repo.create` builds an empty MST, adds any initial records, and signs a commit with `prev: null`.

7. **Loading and syncing.**
   - `Repo.load` reads the head commit, then loads the MST lazily from its root CID.
   - `formatRebase` collapses history into a single new commit with `prev: null`.
   - The sync side is `sync/provider.ts` and `sync/consumer.ts`, together with `data-diff.ts` and `mst/diff.ts`. It produces CAR files and diffs, and lets consumers verify them using the signature and the MST (`verify.ts`).

To build a PDS, expose these operations through the XRPC endpoints `com.atproto.repo.*` (`createRecord`, `putRecord`, `deleteRecord`, `applyWrites`, `getRecord`, `listRecords`) and `com.atproto.sync.*` (`getRepo`, `getCheckout`, `getHead`, `getBlocks`, `getRecord`, `subscribeRepos`).

The error comes from `getFeedGen()` returning undefined. The AppView resolves the feed record's `did` (the FEEDGEN_SERVICE_DID) and looks in that DID document for a service with `id === '#bsky_fg'`, `type === 'BskyFeedGenerator'` and a string http(s) `serviceEndpoint`. You set FEEDGEN_SERVICE_DID to your account's did:plc. That DID document only lists your PDS (`#atproto_pds`) and has no `#bsky_fg` service, so the lookup fails. `describeFeedGenerator` still returns the DID because the skeleton just echoes your env value, and your nginx proxy isn't involved.

To fix it, do one of two things:
- Set FEEDGEN_SERVICE_DID to `did:web:hostingdomain.org`, which is your FEEDGEN_HOSTNAME. Your server then needs to serve `/.well-known/did.json` for that hostname, which the skeleton does when the service DID is a did:web. Republish the feed with the record's `did` set to that value.
- Keep the did:plc and add a `#bsky_fg` service of type `BskyFeedGenerator` to that DID document, with `serviceEndpoint` set to `https://hostingdomain.org`. This means updating the PLC operation, which is more involved.

Keep FEEDGEN_PUBLISHER_DID as your account's did:plc.

Your approach is basically right, with one refinement: you verify the repo's current signed commit and then prove the record is in that commit's MST. (1) Resolve the DID to its DID document and take the atproto signing key (did:key). The identity package does this, and its base-resolver has verifySignature, which uses that key. (2) Fetch a record proof, meaning a CAR file with the commit and the MST path to the record, via com.atproto.sync.getRecord. This is the one commit that covers the record, so you don't search through the repo's commit history. (3) Call `verifyProofs(proofs, claims, did, didKey)` in packages/repo/src/verify.ts. It reads the commit from the CAR root and checks commit.did matches the author's DID. It checks the commit signature against the signing key with util.verifyCommitSig, which calls crypto.verifySignature on the commit's unsigned bytes. It then looks up collection/rkey in the MST and compares the record's CID to the CID of the claimed record. Records the proof supports come back in `verified`, and the rest in `unverified`. `verifyRecords` does the same for a full repo CAR.

There is no endpoint for this. The code has no "get blocked-by" API. The lexicons only have `app.bsky.graph.getBlocks`, which lists the accounts you have blocked. The only "blocked by" signal is `viewer.blockedBy` in `app.bsky.actor.defs#viewerState`. It is a boolean you get for one specific profile, for example from getProfile or getProfiles. Blocks are public `app.bsky.graph.block` records stored in each blocker's repo. To build a full list like Clearsky's, you have to index the network yourself. Nothing in this codebase does that yet. There is no API for sending engagement signals such as dwell time, watch time, or "show more/less" back to a feed. A search for interaction or feedback endpoints found none. The only feed-related calls are `app.bsky.feed.getFeed` and `getFeedSkeleton`.

How it works today:
- The client calls `getFeed` on the appview. The appview resolves the feed generator's endpoint from its DID document, then calls the generator's `app.bsky.feed.getFeedSkeleton`.
- That call takes only `feed`, `limit` and `cursor` (lexicon at `atproto/lexicons/app/bsky/feed/getFeedSkeleton.json`).
- The user's `authorization` header is passed through to the generator, with a `@TODO` noting that this is temporary (`packages/bsky/src/api/app/bsky/feed/getFeed.ts:103-109`). The generator can therefore identify the requesting user.
- The generator returns a list of post URIs plus a cursor.

Because of that, personalisation is up to the feed generator. It can use the requester's DID together with data it already has access to, such as that user's likes, reposts, follows and posts. These are public records, which the generator can read from the firehose or the appview. Signals like time spent on a post are not collected or sent anywhere by the protocol or by Bluesky's appview. A generator that wants them would need its own channel, for example a custom endpoint in the client, which is outside this repo.

The code enforces the object-only rule, but it doesn't say why. I found no comment or doc explaining the rationale, so what follows about reasons is inference.

What the code does:
- `lexRecord` in the lexicon package is defined with `record: lexObject`. It isn't `z.union([lexRefVariant, lexObject])`. A lexicon with `record: {type:'ref'}` therefore fails schema parsing.
- XRPC bodies and subscription messages use `schema: z.union([lexRefVariant, lexObject])`, which is why they can take a `ref` or `union`.
- Record validation relies on the record def being a concrete object. `Lexicons.validate` calls `ComplexValidators.object(this, 'Record', def.record, value)` directly on `def.record`. `assertValidRecord` calls `assertValidRecord(this, def as LexRecord, value)` after checking that `$type` equals the record's own NSID.

Likely problems if `record` could be a ref (my inference):
- The validators would have to resolve the ref first. A union would also let `$type` select a different type than the record's own NSID, which weakens the `$type == collection NSID` check.
- Generated code, where `Record` is an interface built from the object's properties, would need to handle refs and unions.
- A ref to a shared object lets that object change under every record type that uses it.

You can already share a definition without a top-level ref. Define the shared shape as an `object` def, such as `#main`-style or `other.defs#subject`. Then use a `ref` to it for the property inside each record's object. That adds one nesting level, which is the cost you were hoping to avoid.

No. The lexicon string validator applies the format check to any provided string, including "", with no special-casing for empty values. Each format validator (did, handle, cid, uri, at-uri, nsid, datetime, language, at-identifier) rejects "" (e.g. CID.parse("") throws, ensureValid* throw, uri regex requires content). The check runs regardless of required/nullable; only an omitted (undefined) value skips it, or a default is used. So SDKs sending "" for formatted params (like cid in getRecord) will fail validation.

Nothing in this codebase implements phone verification or a captcha for createAccount. "InvalidPhoneVerification" and "verificationCode" appear nowhere in the repo. The createAccount lexicon only accepts email, handle, password, and optionally did, inviteCode and recoveryKey. Its declared errors are InvalidHandle, InvalidPassword, InvalidInviteCode, HandleNotAvailable, UnsupportedDomain, UnresolvableDid and IncompatibleDidDoc. The only gating mechanism a PDS built from this code exposes is an invite code. describeServer reports it as `inviteCodeRequired`.

So the phone/captcha check comes from Bluesky's hosted service (bsky.social), not from the open-source PDS. There is no documented way for a third-party client to satisfy it, because the captcha token is tied to the official client.

Suggestions:
1. Call com.atproto.server.describeServer on the target server to see whether it needs an invite code.
2. Send `inviteCode` in createAccount if one is required.
3. Point your client at a PDS you control or another PDS that doesn't require phone verification. Account creation works there with just handle, email and password, plus an invite code if the server requires one.
4. For bsky.social, have users create the account in the official app or web client, then log in from your client with createSession, ideally using an app password.

You don't build a blobref from the file yourself. Pass the raw bytes (a Buffer or Uint8Array) to uploadBlob with the MIME type as `encoding`. The server stores the blob and returns the blobref in `res.data.blob`. Then use that in your record, for example in an `app.bsky.embed.images` embed. Example: `const file = fs.readFileSync('img.png'); const res = await agent.uploadBlob(file, { encoding: 'image/png' });` then `images: [{ image: res.data.blob, alt: '...' }]`.

Service-auth JWTs (signed with an account's atproto signing key, verified via DID-doc signingKey + aud by services like the AppView, bsky/src/auth.ts verifyJwt) are for service-to-service calls, not for authenticating to your own PDS. The PDS only accepts tokens it issued itself: HS256 JWTs signed/verified with its own jwtSecret (jwt.verify(token, this._secret)) with scope com.atproto.access / appPass / refresh. So a service token yields InvalidToken. For a bot/script, use createSession with an app password (scope com.atproto.appPass), then refreshSession to renew (access 120min, refresh 90 days); app passwords are revocable. No client-credentials/OAuth flow exists in this code.

Question 2 (`$type`): this codebase doesn't settle it as a spec rule, but the evidence is that you should set `$type` in the client. Don't rely on the PDS adding it.

- The reference PDS fills in a missing `$type` itself. `setCollectionName` does `if (!record.$type) { record.$type = collection }`, and `prepareCreate` and `prepareUpdate` both call it. That explains why your requests worked there.
- The PDS only does this as leniency. The `createRecord` lexicon declares `record` as `type: "unknown"` with the description "The record to create." and says nothing about `$type` being optional or auto-added.
- The PDS's own validation (`assertValidRecord`) rejects a record with no string `$type` ("No $type provided"). Tranquil is acting consistently with that.
- The official client already follows this. Every typed `create` helper in `packages/api/src/client/index.ts` sets `record.$type = '...'` before calling `createRecord`. For example, line 1503 does `record.$type = 'app.bsky.feed.post'`.
- My recommendation: have the client always send `$type`. A PDS that also fills it in if missing is a bonus, not something to depend on.
